annotation.reasoning_summary: Polygon features represent discrete housing association property/building-block assets with ownership and dwelling-count attributes. They do not form a complete tessellation, and numeric fields are attributes of the objects rather than the main mapped phenomenon.

All features are points representing distinct archaeological cesspits and finds at addresses. By the point branch, these are countable real-world objects/places, not measurements, events, or numeric amounts.

Point geometries represent distinct archaeological finds/objects in water soils, identified by object code, location, caption, and photos. Decisive rule: point objects/facilities/assets -> ObjectDS, not amount or event.

Polygon features are selected archaeological site areas, not a complete tessellation. Each feature is a named, address-linked archaeological site/vindplaats, so the decisive entity rule is object rather than event or amount.

Polygons mark selected parks/areas with barbecue rules (ban, restrictions, permit) and do not form a complete tessellation of Amsterdam. They are bounded special zones where a regulation applies, so the decisive rule is patch rather than coverage or reporting units.

Polygon layer contains a small set of named protected city/village conservation areas, not a tessellation of Amsterdam. By the object rule for identifiable named bounded entities such as protected cityscapes, the entity is ObjectDS.

Point geometries represent wild bee observations at named areas with a year and observed species. Using the event rule, observations tied to occurrence time are classified as EventDS rather than objects or amounts.

The layer contains point features for honey bee hive/colony locations. The numeric fields count hives/colonies, but the points primarily represent beekeeping sites or hive objects with attributes, so the point object rule applies rather than AmountDS.

Polygons represent an area-wide soil quality zoning/classification layer with categorical soil function and quality classes, intended as thematic coverage rather than discrete objects or numeric amounts. Region tessellation and coverage rules apply.

The layer contains point features, each representing an individual tree with species, tree number, height, owner, and manager attributes. Numeric fields like planting year and radius are attributes of the tree objects, not the main mapped phenomenon.

The layer contains point features representing individual trees with identifiers, species, height, planting year, owner and manager. Numeric fields are attributes of tree objects, so the point object rule applies rather than amount or measurement.

The layer contains point features representing individual trees, identifiable real-world objects with species, tree number, owner, height and planting year attributes. Numeric fields are object attributes, not the main mapped phenomenon.

The layer contains point features representing individual trees with identifiers, species, height, owner/manager, and planting year. These are distinct real-world objects; numeric fields are attributes, not the main mapped phenomenon.

The layer contains point locations for neighborhood compost facilities/initiatives, each representing a distinct real-world place or asset. Numeric fields like number of residents and start year are attributes, not the main mapped phenomenon, so the point object rule applies.
The layer contains polygon camera surveillance areas that are selected bounded zones, not a complete tessellation or reporting units. Entity is PatchDS by the special-zone/phenomenon-patch rule.

Point geometries represent individual Canadian poplar trees identified by tree number and species. Planning and measure fields are attributes of these tree objects, so the decisive rule is object rather than event or amount.

The layer contains point features representing distinct crowd-monitoring sensor/camera assets with object numbers, type, power, rotation, and active status. Numeric rotation is an object attribute, so the decisive rule is point objects/facilities -> ObjectDS.

Polygon features mark selected named areas where cultural-historical explorations apply; they do not form a full tessellation or reporting-unit coverage. Decisive rule: bounded selected phenomenon areas/patches rather than objects or amounts.

All features are points, and the layer maps locations where knotweed is present. Species and area values are attributes of these occurrence locations, so the decisive rule is point-based presence/existence rather than amount.

Point geometries represent distinct ecopassage/bottleneck locations and proposed or realized wildlife crossing solutions. Numeric/year/status fields are attributes of these objects/projects, so the object rule applies rather than amount or event.

Polygon/MultiPolygon features are selected potential wind-energy zones, not a complete tessellation. The decisive entity rule is patch: bounded special/phenomenon areas with capacity/yield as attributes, not numeric amount as the main feature.

All features are point geometries. Each point primarily represents a stemlocatie/polling location or voting district location; vote counts and percentages are attributes of those polling-place objects, so the decisive rule is object rather than amount.

The layer consists of point features marking individual oak processionary caterpillar nest/tree locations. The decisive rule is object: each point represents a distinct countable real-world nest/location, while priority, height, and mutation date are attributes rather than the main phenomenon.

Polygon features represent selected pedicab regulation/restriction areas, not a complete tessellation or reporting units. They are bounded special zones where rules apply, so the decisive rule is patch.

The layer contains point features representing distinct pedicab/coach stand pitches (standplaatsen), which are identifiable facilities/places. By the point object rule, this is ObjectDS rather than an amount or event layer.

Features are point locations for non-residential address/function objects such as offices, churches, shops, and horeca. Numeric fields like floor area are attributes, but the decisive rule is object/facility representation, not amount.

Polygons classify the city into function-mix categories (wonen/voorzieningen/werken) with CAT and percentage fields, indicating an area-wide thematic coverage. The polygons are intended as a tessellated thematic partition rather than discrete object patches; numeric fields support the classification but are not the main entity as AmountDS.

The layer contains neighborhood polygons that form an administrative partition of Amsterdam, so geometry is a tessellation. Neighborhoods are reporting/administrative units used to attach attributes, so the entity is LatticeDS; the area field is only an attribute.

Neighborhood polygons form an administrative/statistical partition of Amsterdam excluding water, so geometry is a tessellation. As buurtcombinaties/neighborhood units used to attach codes and area attributes, the entity is a reporting unit/lattice, not an amount despite Opp_m2.

The layer represents Amsterdam neighbourhood polygons that form an administrative partition of the city, so the geometry is a tessellation. Neighbourhoods are reporting/administrative units with attached attributes, so the entity is LatticeDS.

Neighborhood polygons are administrative/reporting units that form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam excluding water, so geometry is a tessellation and entity is a lattice/reporting unit. The area field is only an attribute, not the main phenomenon.
City districts are administrative/reporting units that partition Amsterdam; polygon regions form a tessellation, and the area field is just an attribute rather than the main phenomenon.

City districts are administrative/reporting regions that partition Amsterdam (excluding water), so the polygon geometry is a tessellation and the entity is a lattice/reporting unit. The area field is only an attribute, not the main phenomenon.

The layer contains polygon administrative areas ('22 Gebieden') with area and district codes, intended to partition Amsterdam into reporting/administrative units. Thus geometry is a tessellation and entity is LatticeDS despite numeric area attributes.

Polygons represent Amsterdam's 22 named administrative/statistical areas excluding water, forming a near-complete partition of the city; by the reporting-unit rule this is a tessellation with LatticeDS entity. Numeric area is only an attribute.

Polygons are named Amsterdam practice areas forming an area division/near-complete tessellation of the municipality. They function as administrative or reporting units; the area field is just an attribute, not the main phenomenon.

The polygons are named Amsterdam practice areas excluding water, intended as an administrative/reporting subdivision of the city. They form a near-complete partition, so geometry is VectorTessellation; as reporting/administrative units with attributes like area and district code, entity is LatticeDS.
Polygon features are industrial noise contour areas such as 50 dB zones, not a full tessellation. The decisive rule is contour: regions represent noise value bands/contours around industrial areas.

Polygon layer represents aviation noise contour zones with dB interval classes (e.g., 55–60 dB, 60–65 dB), so the decisive rule is contour/value bands. The polygons are selected contour areas rather than a complete tessellation of Amsterdam.

Polygons represent traffic noise contour zones by dB class (e.g., 50-55, >70 dB), i.e. interval bands of a measured field rather than reporting units or objects. They are bounded contour areas, not a complete tessellation.
Polygons represent traffic noise contour zones by dB interval classes (e.g., 50–55 dB, 55–60 dB), not reporting units or a full-area tessellation. Decisive rule: contour/band class representation.

Point geometries represent polling locations/stembureaus. Although many vote counts and percentages are attached, these are attributes of polling station objects; the point object rule applies rather than AmountDS.

The layer contains point features for individual green roof/roof garden locations with addresses and roof types. Numeric fields like area and year are attributes of these objects, so the point-object rule applies rather than AmountDS.
Land use polygons form an area-wide thematic classification, so geometry is a tessellation and entity follows the coverage rule rather than amount despite area/code fields.
The layer contains point features for named historical buildings/structures such as churches and gates. These are distinct real-world objects with temporal attributes, not events or numeric amounts.

The layer contains polygon municipality/administrative areas identified by GEMEENTE_ID. Administrative polygons are treated as a tessellation of units, and as reporting/administrative units they classify as LatticeDS rather than AmountDS despite numeric IDs.

Polygon areas mark selected dog off-leash, restriction, and ban zones; they do not form a complete tessellation of Amsterdam. By the region branch, these are bounded special zones/phenomenon patches rather than reporting units, objects, or full coverage.

Polygon features are selected named green-structure areas (parks, cemeteries, sport parks, corridors) and do not form a complete tessellation of Amsterdam. By the object rule, these are identifiable managed green spaces/places; area fields are only attributes, not the main mapped amount.

Features are point locations of individual private elm trees, which are distinct real-world objects. Numeric/categorical fields like planting year, diameter, and height are attributes of the trees, not the main mapped amount.
Point geometries represent named youth/student housing complexes or projects. The dwelling count is an attribute of these objects, not the main mapped phenomenon, so the point object rule applies.

The layer contains point features representing individual chestnut trees, with species and disease status as attributes. By the point-object rule, these are distinct real-world objects rather than point measurements or numeric amounts.
Point geometries represent drought-related groundwater/elevation measurements (GLG, maaiveld) at sampled locations, so the decisive rule is point measurement of a continuous environmental phenomenon.

Polygon features classify flood probability and depth categories across the area, so the regions are best treated as an area-wide thematic tessellation/coverage rather than discrete objects or reporting units.

Point geometries represent named market locations such as Albert Cuypmarkt and Waterlooplein. The decisive rule is object: each feature is a distinct real-world place/facility, with opening days and article types as attributes rather than the main phenomenon.

The layer contains point features for named green monuments such as parks and gardens. Each point represents a distinct real-world monument/object; the numeric monument number is an identifier, not an amount.
Point geometries represent individual monumental trees, which are distinct real-world objects/assets. Numeric and categorical attributes describe the trees but are not the main mapped phenomenon.

All features are point geometries representing individual monuments/buildings or heritage objects with names, status, addresses, and monument identifiers. By the point object rule, these are discrete real-world objects; numeric monument numbers are identifiers, not mapped amounts.
All features are point locations. The layer primarily maps the presence of quay wall plant species at locations; annual counts are attributes and do not make the numeric amount the main phenomenon.

The layer contains MultiPolygon features that do not appear to form an area-wide tessellation, so the geometry is PlainVectorRegion. The mapped phenomenon is NO2 air-quality measurements over 4-week periods, i.e. sampled values of a continuous environmental phenomenon, so the entity follows the point-measurement rule rather than treating the numeric fields as generic amounts.

Point geometries represent NO2 air-quality measurement locations; by the measurement-layer priority rule, point locations sampling a continuous environmental phenomenon are PointMeasuresDS rather than ordinary objects.

Polygon features mark selected bounded areas of the primeval gulch phenomenon with category codes; they do not form a full tessellation or reporting units, so this is a non-exhaustive patch/zone layer.

Point geometries represent sounding/borehole measurement locations with depth/elevation values such as Top_Pleistoceen, sampling a subsurface continuous phenomenon; decisive rule is point measurement layer.

Polygon features are selected development neighbourhoods (19 named/code areas) and do not form a complete tessellation of Amsterdam. They are identifiable named bounded development areas, so the decisive rule is object rather than reporting-unit lattice or full coverage.
Features are point locations of distinct public toilet facilities/assets. Numeric price is only an attribute, so the decisive rule is point object rather than amount.

Polygon features represent selected overnight-policy areas with categories such as NIET/TENZIJ and conditions, not a full citywide tessellation or numeric amount layer. Decisive rule: selected bounded policy/phenomenon zones -> patch.

Polygon layer classifies areas into parking-standard categories A/B/C, functioning like an area-wide zoning/policy classification. The regions are intended as a tessellation, and the entity is a coverage rather than discrete objects or reporting units.

Polygons represent discrete named parks, plantsoenen, and recreational green spaces, not a complete tessellation of Amsterdam. The area field is an attribute of these managed bounded objects, so the decisive rule is object rather than amount.

Polygon postcode-4 areas are intended to partition the city into postcode/reporting units, so geometry is a tessellation. Entity is LatticeDS because postcode areas are administrative/statistical reporting units; the area field is only an attribute.

Postcode4 polygons are postcode/reporting areas that form a near-complete partition of the study area excluding water, so geometry is a tessellation and entity is a lattice/reporting unit despite numeric area attributes.
Postcode6 polygon areas are intended to partition the city into postcode reporting units; by the tessellation and reporting-unit rules, geometry is VectorTessellation and entity is LatticeDS.

The layer contains LineString features representing plus/main transport infrastructure networks for walking, cycling, tram, bus, and auto. By the network priority rule, connected route/transport infrastructure is NetworkDS; numeric fields like speed are attributes, not the main phenomenon.

Polygons represent discrete pedestrian-related places such as parks and squares, not a complete tessellation of Amsterdam. Under the region object rule, parks/squares are identifiable bounded real-world places rather than reporting units, coverage, or amount values.

The layer contains point features for named mast locations with privacy statement links. Each point represents a distinct real-world asset/location, so the decisive rule is point object rather than amount, event, or measurement.

The layer contains point features marking specific privacy-related research/pilot locations or items. These are distinct mapped places/activities with privacy statements, not measurements or numeric amounts; by the point object rule this is ObjectDS.

Point features represent distinct named car-fleet scan/privacy locations with addresses and lane information. They are identifiable locations/assets, not sampled continuous measurements or numeric amounts, so the object rule applies.

Features are point polling locations/stemdistricts for the 2019 election. The vote counts and percentages are numeric attributes of these polling-place objects; per the object rule, polling stations with vote totals are not AmountDS.

Polygon features represent selected Rainproof groundwater/drainage zones rather than administrative/reporting units or a complete tessellation. The drainage category describes special bounded areas where a condition applies, so the decisive rule is patch rather than coverage or amount.

Polygon hydro units appear to divide the Rainproof study area into numbered planning/reporting units. The HYDRO_ID is an identifier, not a mapped amount, so the decisive rules are tessellation geometry and reporting-unit/lattice entity.

Polygon features mark selected Rainproof bottleneck/problem areas and do not form a complete tessellation. They are bounded affected zones with urgency attributes, so the decisive rule is patch rather than reporting unit, coverage, object, or amount.

Polygon features list selected named locations for polder sewerage in the Rainproof layer; they do not form a complete tessellation. They are best treated as bounded special/phenomenon areas rather than reporting units or full coverage, so PatchDS.

The layer contains point locations for distinct religious buildings/places of worship with names, addresses, building types, denominations, and websites. These are identifiable real-world facilities/objects; the numeric category id is only an attribute, not an amount phenomenon.

LineString features represent sidewalk/street segments with width and obstruction attributes. By the network rule, sidewalk segments are part of a pedestrian route/street infrastructure system; numeric width/count fields are attributes, not the main entity.

The layer contains LineString features representing selected street/roadway segments where moped roadway rules apply. By the priority rule for route/street/transport infrastructure, this is a line network layer rather than an amount or event layer.

All features are points representing distinct public sport/playground facilities with names and facility attributes. The numeric surface area is only an object attribute, so the object rule applies rather than amount.

The layer contains point locations for named city farming sites with address, type, status, initiator, and website. Each point represents a distinct real-world place/facility, so by the point object rule it is ObjectDS.

Polygons are discrete named city-farming terrains/garden parks with addresses and websites, not a complete tessellation or reporting units. Decisive rule: identifiable bounded real-world places/managed terrains -> ObjectDS.

The layer contains point features for individual city-pilot initiatives/organizations and their activities, with year and sector as attributes. These are distinct real-world initiatives/places rather than numeric amounts or sampled measurements, so the point-object rule applies.

The layer contains LineString features representing major city streets/head streets, i.e. a street/route infrastructure system. By the network rule, connected street or transport line systems are NetworkDS.
LineString features represent district heating/cooling transport infrastructure. By the network rule for connected utility/transport lines, this is a LineDS with NetworkDS entity.

Polygon features mark selected district heating/cooling neighbourhood/service areas with net type and status, not a complete city tessellation. Decisive rule: bounded utility phenomenon zones/patches rather than reporting units or full coverage.

Polygons are selected housing development/project areas, not a complete tessellation. Features have project names and represent identifiable housing plan areas; dwelling counts are attributes, so object rule applies rather than AmountDS.

The layer contains point locations for named farms, markets, shops, and horeca places offering local products. Each feature primarily represents a distinct real-world business/place, so by the point object rule it is ObjectDS, not an amount or event layer.
LineString features represent tram and metro lines, a connected public transport route system; decisive rule is network for transport lines.
The layer contains LineString features representing tram and metro lines, which are a connected public transport route system; by the network rule this is NetworkDS.

Point geometries represent distinct real-world tram stops and metro stations. Although tied to transport lines, each feature is a stop/station object rather than a line network, and numeric radius is only an attribute.

The layer contains point features representing distinct tram stops and metro stations, which are identifiable transport facilities. Although related to a transport network, each feature is a stop/station object rather than connected line infrastructure.

The layer contains point features representing distinct traffic light installations/intersections, i.e. identifiable real-world assets. Numeric year/status fields are attributes of those objects, not the main mapped amount.

LineString features represent road/link segments, but the layer is specifically traffic prognoses with forecast traffic volumes by period and vehicle type. Using the line amount rule, the numeric traffic intensity/forecast is the main mapped phenomenon rather than merely an attribute of a road network.

Point geometries represent distinct polling locations (Stemlocatie). Vote totals and percentages are attributes of those polling station objects; decisive rule is object over amount for polling stations with vote totals.

The layer contains point features representing individual trees identified by BOOM_ID and species/planting attributes. These are distinct real-world objects; numeric fields like planting year and size classes are attributes, not the main mapped amount.

Point geometries represent distinct traffic information system assets such as TV cameras, DRIP displays, and other equipment with object numbers and locations. Numeric fields are attributes of these objects, not the main mapped phenomenon.

Point geometries represent distinct traffic information/access-control assets (BFA installations such as barriers/pollers) with identifiers, type, location, management, and installation year. Numeric fields are object attributes, so the decisive rule is point object/facility rather than amount or network.

All features are points. The layer maps breeding bird occurrences/observations at locations with year-specific counts, so the decisive rule is the event/occurrence rule rather than treating the count fields as AmountDS.
Features are point locations for individual Vondelpark benches, which are distinct real-world assets. Numeric rotation is only an object attribute, so the point object rule applies.

LineString features represent street segments (Straatvaknummer) with walkability and crowding attributes. By the network priority rule, a street/route system with attributes is classified as NetworkDS rather than AmountDS or CoverageDS.

Point features represent distinct wall-art artworks with title, artist, technique, address, and heritage attributes. Numeric year fields are object attributes, not the main mapped phenomenon; decisive rule is point object.

Polygons categorize areas by welstand/building review level using categorical fields, functioning like an area-wide policy/thematic classification. This fits tessellation geometry and CoverageDS rather than discrete objects or numeric amounts.

Polygon layer with categorical 'Systeemnaam' classes representing area-wide building/aesthetic policy systems, similar to a zoning or thematic classification. The regions are intended as a tessellated coverage rather than discrete objects or numeric amounts.

The layer contains point features marking WWII attack-related occurrences at addresses, with date, type, and description. By the event rule, the main phenomenon is something that happened in time, so the entity is EventDS.

Polygons represent discrete housing development plans/projects, not a complete tessellation. Dwelling totals and phases are attributes of project objects, so the decisive rule is object rather than amount or event.

Point geometries represent distinct self-build plot/projects or development locations. Numeric fields such as dwelling counts or plot area are attributes of these objects, so the object rule applies rather than amount or event.

The layer uses polygon roof/building-like areas related to solar panels on heritage, not a complete tessellation of Amsterdam. The features are best understood as discrete bounded real-world roof/heritage objects with a category attribute, rather than reporting units or a numeric amount layer.

The layer contains point features representing detected solar panel installations/locations, with counts and power as attributes. By the point-object rule, these are discrete real-world assets rather than numeric magnitudes as the sole phenomenon.

The layer contains point features for named swimming locations such as pools, beaches, and water play areas. Each point represents a distinct real-world place/facility, so by the point object rule it is ObjectDS.
